title: AMO-Bench: Large Language Models Still Struggle in High School Math Competitions
extended_summary:
This paper introduces AMO-Bench, a new benchmark for evaluating advanced mathematical reasoning in large language models (LLMs). The authors argue that existing high school math competition benchmarks such as AIME and HMMT are increasingly saturated, making them less useful for distinguishing top-tier models, and that some may also be vulnerable to memorization or leakage. AMO-Bench is designed to address these issues by providing 50 entirely original, human-crafted problems that are cross-validated to meet at least IMO-level difficulty standards.

The benchmark is not an educational intervention in the classroom sense, but an evaluation resource for K-12 mathematics competition-style reasoning. The included problems span algebraic equations and inequalities, functions and sequences, geometry, number theory, and combinatorics. Each item requires only a final answer rather than a full proof, allowing automatic grading; the paper also includes human-annotated solution paths and a grading pipeline using parser-based or LLM-based scoring depending on answer type.

Experiments on 26 LLMs show that even the strongest model achieves only 52.4% accuracy on AMO-Bench, with most models below 40%. The authors conclude that current LLMs still struggle with these harder olympiad-level problems, though performance improves with more test-time compute and higher output-token budgets. The paper’s main contribution is therefore a benchmark and evaluation methodology rather than a study of student learning or educational implementation.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a benchmark construction and model evaluation paper, not a K-12 intervention study. It reports no student-level causal design, comparator, or educational outcome evidence relevant to classroom effectiveness.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not test impact on learners or instruction; it only measures LLM performance on advanced math benchmark items. Any educational impact is indirect and not established as a K-12 effect.

interventions.use_case: A mathematical reasoning benchmark for evaluating large language models on original Olympiad-level and higher math competition problems with final-answer grading

finding.finding_summary: Across 26 LLMs evaluated on AMO-Bench (n=26 models; 50 problems), the best-performing model (GPT-5-Thinking High) reached only 52.4% accuracy, and most models scored below 40%, indicating substantial difficulty on advanced mathematical reasoning tasks. At the same time, performance improved with greater test-time compute: top models showed a near-linear increase in AVG@32 as output length increased, and pass@32 exceeded 70% for top-tier reasoning models, suggesting meaningful headroom for further gains.
finding.measure: Accuracy on AMO-Bench; AVG@32; pass@k under varying test-time compute/output length
